subject: Anatomy
title: Upper Limb

source.book: Recall by Yanal — Upper & Lower Limb Anatomy
source.title: Upper Limb

objectives: Identify the key structures of Upper Limb at each level of dissection.
Relate the nerves, vessels and muscles of Upper Limb to their functions.
Localise the named spaces and regions of Upper Limb and list their contents.
Recognise the common clinical lesions associated with Upper Limb.
Reproduce the high-yield relations of Upper Limb tested in vivas and MCQs.

glossary.def: C5-C6 branch of the posterior cord; supplies deltoid and teres minor, sensation over the regimental badge area.
Largest branch of the posterior cord (C5-T1); extensor supply to arm and forearm; injured in mid-shaft humeral fracture.
C6-T1 nerve of the anterior forearm and thenar muscles; compressed in carpal tunnel syndrome.
C8-T1 nerve to most intrinsic hand muscles; injured at the medial epicondyle and in Guyon's canal.
Lateral-cord nerve (C5-C7) piercing coracobrachialis to supply the anterior arm.
Network of C5-T1 ventral rami: roots, trunks, divisions, cords, branches.
Supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis stabilising the glenohumeral joint.
Fibro-osseous space deep to the flexor retinaculum transmitting the median nerve and long flexor tendons.
Triangular hollow anterior to the elbow containing the brachial artery, median nerve and biceps tendon.
Depression at the wrist bounded by EPL and APB/EPB tendons; floor is the scaphoid.
Continuation of the axillary artery in the arm; divides into radial and ulnar arteries in the cubital fossa.
Muscle bulk at the base of the thumb (APB, FPB, opponens pollicis); median-innervated.
Rotator-cuff muscle initiating abduction; tendon wears in impingement.
Upper-trunk (C5-C6) injury giving the waiter's-tip posture.
Lower-trunk (C8-T1) injury causing a claw hand.
Median-nerve compression at the wrist; nocturnal paraesthesia in the radial 3.5 digits.
Long-thoracic-nerve (serratus anterior) palsy causing medial scapular winging.
Distal radial fracture with dorsal displacement (dinner-fork deformity).
Fall on the outstretched hand; risk of avascular necrosis of the proximal pole.
Ball-and-socket shoulder joint; most mobile and most commonly dislocated (usually anteroinferior).
Fibrous band roofing the carpal tunnel between the carpal eminences.
Superficial vein of the lateral arm draining to the axillary vein via the deltopectoral groove.
Tapping over a nerve to reproduce tingling in its distribution; used at the carpal tunnel.
Strip of skin supplied by a single spinal nerve root.

cards.front: Extensor carpi radialis brevis — nerve supply?

cards.front: Extensor carpi radialis brevis — main action(s)?

cards.front: Musculocutaneous nerve — which muscle does it pierce?
cards.back: Coracobrachialis
The anterior compartment of the arm: coracobrachialis, biceps brachii and brachialis (the 'BBC')
Continues as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm (skin of the lateral forearm)
Weak elbow flexion and supination; loss of the biceps reflex; sensory loss over the lateral forearm

cards.front: Axillary nerve — root value and origin?
cards.back: C5, C6 — from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus
Passes through the quadrangular space with the posterior circumflex humeral artery, winding around the surgical neck of the humerus
Deltoid and teres minor
Upper lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm — the 'regimental badge' area over the deltoid

cards.front: Axillary nerve — two classic causes of injury?
cards.back: Surgical neck of humerus fracture and anterior (inferior) shoulder dislocation
Impaired abduction of the arm (loss of deltoid) and weak lateral rotation

cards.front: Radial nerve — root value and origin?
cards.back: C5–T1 — the largest branch of the posterior cord

cards.front: Radial nerve — course in the arm?
cards.back: Runs in the radial (spiral) groove of the humerus with the profunda brachii artery, between the medial and lateral heads of triceps
All extensors: triceps and anconeus in the arm; brachioradialis, ECRL and supinator, then the posterior interosseous nerve supplies the rest of the extensor compartment
Posterior arm and forearm, and the dorsum of the lateral 3½ digits (proximal to the nail beds) via the superficial radial nerve

cards.front: Radial nerve — deformity with a mid-shaft humeral fracture?
cards.back: Wrist drop — loss of wrist and finger extensors (the posterior interosseous/deep branch)
Compression in the radial groove (e.g. arm over a chair back), causing wrist drop

cards.front: Posterior interosseous nerve — what does injury spare?
cards.back: Sensation (it is purely motor) and wrist extension is preserved via ECRL, so there is finger drop without true wrist drop

cards.front: Median nerve — root value and origin?
cards.back: C6–T1 — formed by lateral and medial roots from the lateral and medial cords

cards.front: Median nerve — branches in the arm?
cards.back: None — it gives no branches in the arm

cards.front: Median nerve — motor supply in the forearm?
cards.back: Most anterior forearm flexors EXCEPT flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus

cards.front: Median nerve — the 'LOAF' muscles in the hand?
cards.back: Lateral two Lumbricals, Opponens pollicis, Abductor pollicis brevis, Flexor pollicis brevis

cards.front: Median nerve — anterior interosseous branch supplies?
cards.back: Flexor pollicis longus, pronator quadratus and the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus
Palmar skin of the lateral 3½ digits and adjacent palm; palmar cutaneous branch supplies the thenar skin (spared in carpal tunnel syndrome)

cards.front: Median nerve — deformity of a HIGH lesion (at the elbow)?
cards.back: Hand of benediction on attempted fist (loss of lateral finger flexion) and 'ape hand' (thenar wasting, thumb adducted)

cards.front: Median nerve — carpal tunnel (LOW) lesion signs?
cards.back: Thenar wasting, loss of thumb opposition/abduction, sensory loss over the lateral 3½ fingertips (thenar skin spared)

cards.front: Ulnar nerve — root value and origin?
cards.back: C8, T1 — the terminal branch of the medial cord

cards.front: Ulnar nerve — course at the elbow?
cards.back: Passes behind the medial epicondyle (the 'funny bone'), where it is superficial and easily injured

cards.front: Ulnar nerve — motor supply in the forearm?
cards.back: Flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus

cards.front: Ulnar nerve — motor supply in the hand?
cards.back: Most intrinsic muscles: hypothenar muscles, all interossei, medial two lumbricals, adductor pollicis and palmaris brevis
Medial 1½ digits (palmar and dorsal) and the adjacent medial palm and hand dorsum

cards.front: Ulnar nerve — deformity of a LOW lesion (at the wrist)?
cards.back: Claw hand ('main en griffe') — hyperextended MCPs and flexed IPs of the ring and little fingers
A HIGHER (elbow) ulnar lesion produces LESS clawing than a lower lesion, because FDP to the medial fingers is also paralysed so the fingers flex less

cards.front: Froment's sign — what does it test?
cards.back: Adductor pollicis (ulnar nerve): the thumb IP flexes (FPL, median) to grip paper when adduction is weak
C5, C6, C7 ('wings of heaven C5–7')
Serratus anterior
Winging of the scapula (medial border lifts off the chest), and inability to raise the arm above the horizontal

cards.front: Suprascapular nerve — origin and root value?
cards.back: Upper trunk of the brachial plexus, C5–C6
Supraspinatus and infraspinatus

cards.front: Suprascapular nerve — where can it be entrapped?
cards.back: At the suprascapular notch (beneath the superior transverse scapular ligament)
C5
Rhomboid major, rhomboid minor and levator scapulae

cards.front: Thoracodorsal nerve — origin and root value?
cards.back: Posterior cord, C6–C8
Latissimus dorsi (at risk in axillary node clearance)
Anterior (ventral) rami of C5, C6, C7, C8 and T1

cards.front: Brachial plexus — order of parts from proximal to distal?
cards.back: Roots → Trunks → Divisions → Cords → Branches ('Real Texans Drink Cold Beer')
Upper (C5–C6), middle (C7) and lower (C8–T1)
Each of the three trunks splits into an anterior and a posterior division (3 + 3)

cards.front: Brachial plexus — the three cords and how they are named?
cards.back: Lateral, medial and posterior cords — named by position around the second part of the axillary artery

cards.front: Brachial plexus — which cord gives the musculocutaneous nerve?
cards.back: The lateral cord

cards.front: Brachial plexus — which cord gives the ulnar nerve?
cards.back: The medial cord
Upper subscapular, thoracodorsal, Lower subscapular, Radial, Axillary ('ULTRA')

cards.front: Brachial plexus — branches directly from the roots?
cards.back: Dorsal scapular nerve (C5) and long thoracic nerve (C5–C7)

cards.front: Brachial plexus — branches from the upper trunk?
cards.back: Suprascapular nerve and the nerve to subclavius

cards.front: Brachial plexus — how is the median nerve formed?
cards.back: By a lateral root (lateral cord) and a medial root (medial cord) uniting anterior to the axillary artery
The C5–C6 union forming the upper trunk; the classic site of Erb–Duchenne (upper) palsy
An S-shaped long bone; the only long bone to ossify in membrane and the first bone in the body to begin ossifying
Junction of the middle and lateral thirds (the weakest point); the medial fragment is pulled up by sternocleidomastoid
On the inferior surface laterally — attachment for the coracoclavicular ligament (conoid + trapezoid parts)
The only bony articulation between the upper limb and the axial skeleton (via the sternoclavicular joint); acts as a strut holding the limb away from the trunk
Superior, medial (vertebral) and lateral (axillary) borders
Superior, inferior and lateral angles (the lateral angle bears the glenoid cavity)
Spine, acromion and coracoid process
Shallow pear-shaped socket at the lateral angle for the head of the humerus; deepened by the glenoid labrum
On the superior border medial to the coracoid; transmits the suprascapular nerve (artery passes above the ligament)
Origin of the long head of biceps (supraglenoid) and long head of triceps (infraglenoid)
The head articulates at the glenoid; the anatomical neck is the old epiphyseal line just distal to the head
Junction of the head/tubercles with the shaft; a common fracture site related to the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery
Greater tubercle (lateral) — insertions of supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor; Lesser tubercle (anterior) — insertion of subscapularis
Lodges the tendon of the long head of biceps; latissimus dorsi (floor/medial lip), pectoralis major (lateral lip), teres major (medial lip) attach around it
Oblique groove on the posterior shaft carrying the radial nerve and profunda brachii artery
Roughening on the lateral mid-shaft for insertion of the deltoid
Capitulum (lateral) articulates with the radial head; trochlea (medial) articulates with the trochlear notch of the ulna
Common flexor origin; the ulnar nerve runs behind it (fracture endangers the ulnar nerve)
Common extensor origin (site of tennis elbow)
Disc-shaped proximal head that articulates with the capitulum and, at its rim, the radial notch of the ulna within the annular ligament
Just distal to the neck; insertion of the biceps brachii tendon
Distal lateral projection; extends more distally than the ulnar styloid (lost in Colles' fracture)
On the dorsal distal radius; the tendon of extensor pollicis longus hooks around it
The point of the elbow; insertion of triceps; forms the upper part of the trochlear notch
Anterior projection forming the lower trochlear notch; brachialis inserts on its tuberosity
Articulates with the trochlea of the humerus (the humero-ulnar hinge)
On the lateral coronoid; articulates with the head of the radius (proximal radio-ulnar joint)
The head is DISTAL (opposite to the radius) and bears the styloid process medially
Eight carpal bones in two rows of four
Scaphoid, Lunate, Triquetrum, Pisiform ('Some Lovers Try Positions')
Trapezium, Trapezoid, Capitate, Hamate ('That They Can't Handle')
Most commonly fractured carpal bone; risk of avascular necrosis of the proximal pole (retrograde blood supply); tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox
The most commonly DISLOCATED carpal bone; may compress the median nerve in the carpal tunnel
Bears a hook (hamulus) forming the medial wall of the carpal tunnel and Guyon's canal; near the ulnar nerve
Five metacarpals; each finger has proximal, middle and distal phalanges — the thumb has only proximal and distal phalanges
Saddle-type synovial joint (functions as a ball-and-socket); the only bony link between the upper limb and axial skeleton
Contains an articular disc and is very strong — dislocation is rare despite a wide range of movement
Plane-type synovial joint between the acromion and the lateral clavicle
The coracoclavicular ligament (conoid + trapezoid); its rupture causes shoulder separation with a 'step' deformity
Ball-and-socket synovial joint; the most MOBILE and the most commonly DISLOCATED joint in the body, but inherently unstable

cards.front: Glenohumeral joint — what deepens the socket?
cards.back: The fibrocartilaginous glenoid labrum around the shallow glenoid cavity
The rotator cuff (SITS muscles) reinforcing the capsule on all sides except inferiorly

cards.front: Glenohumeral joint — weakest part / usual dislocation direction?
cards.back: Inferiorly (unsupported by cuff); dislocation is usually antero-inferior, risking the axillary nerve

cards.front: Glenohumeral joint — the three glenohumeral ligaments and coracohumeral ligament?
cards.back: Reinforce the anterior capsule (superior, middle, inferior glenohumeral ligaments) and the superior capsule (coracohumeral)
A hinge synovial joint: humero-ulnar (trochlea–trochlear notch) and humero-radial (capitulum–radial head)
Radial (lateral) collateral ligament and ulnar (medial) collateral ligament resist varus and valgus stress
The lateral (valgus) angle between arm and forearm when extended and supinated (~5–15°, greater in females)

cards.front: Proximal radio-ulnar joint — type and ligament?
cards.back: Pivot synovial joint; the radial head is held against the radial notch by the annular ligament
Pivot synovial joint with an articular disc uniting the ulnar head and the ulnar notch of the radius
Pronation and supination (the radius rotates over a fixed ulna); the interosseous membrane also transfers force from radius to ulna
Ellipsoid (condyloid) synovial joint between the distal radius + articular disc and the scaphoid, lunate and triquetrum
Flexion, extension, abduction (radial deviation) and adduction (ulnar deviation); the ulna does NOT directly take part

cards.front: First carpometacarpal joint — type and importance?
cards.back: Saddle synovial joint (trapezium–1st metacarpal) that allows opposition, giving the human hand its precision grip
The cervico-axillary canal — bounded by the clavicle, the first rib and the superior border of the scapula (gateway for vessels/nerves)
Pectoralis major, pectoralis minor and subclavius (with the clavipectoral fascia)
Subscapularis, teres major and latissimus dorsi
Serratus anterior over the upper ribs and intercostal muscles
The intertubercular groove of the humerus (a narrow bony wall)
Axillary artery and vein, cords/branches of the brachial plexus, axillary lymph nodes and fat

cards.front: Clavipectoral fascia — four structures that pierce it?
cards.back: Cephalic vein, thoraco-acromial artery, lateral pectoral nerve and lymphatics ('a Little To Come Later')
Superiorly a line between the epicondyles; laterally brachioradialis; medially pronator teres; floor is brachialis + supinator; roof is deep fascia + bicipital aponeurosis

cards.front: Cubital fossa — contents lateral to medial?
cards.back: Biceps Tendon, brachial Artery, median Nerve ('TAN'); the radial nerve lies deep at the lateral edge
Site for the brachial pulse, venepuncture of the median cubital vein and measuring blood pressure
Teres minor above, teres major below, long head of triceps medially, surgical neck of humerus laterally
Axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery
Teres minor above, teres major below, long head of triceps laterally; transmits the circumflex scapular artery
Teres major above, long head of triceps medially, lateral head of triceps/humerus laterally; transmits the radial nerve and profunda brachii artery
Floor and walls are the carpal bones (arched); the roof is the flexor retinaculum (transverse carpal ligament)

cards.front: Carpal tunnel — ten structures passing through?
cards.back: The median nerve plus nine tendons: 4 of FDS, 4 of FDP and 1 of flexor pollicis longus

cards.front: Carpal tunnel — what does NOT pass through it?
cards.back: The ulnar nerve and artery (they pass superficial to the retinaculum in Guyon's canal), and the palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve
Between the pisiform and the hook of hamate, superficial to the flexor retinaculum; transmits the ulnar nerve and artery
Laterally abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis; medially extensor pollicis longus; floor is the scaphoid and trapezium

cards.front: Anatomical snuffbox — contents and clinical relevance?
cards.back: The radial artery crosses its floor; deep tenderness suggests a scaphoid fracture
Surrounds the long flexor tendons in the carpal tunnel; continuous with the little-finger digital sheath (infection can spread proximally)
The synovial sheath of flexor pollicis longus; the two bursae may communicate, allowing a 'horseshoe' abscess
Continues the subclavian artery at the lateral border of the first rib and becomes the brachial artery at the inferior border of teres major

cards.front: Axillary artery — how is it divided into 3 parts?
cards.back: By pectoralis minor: first part proximal, second part deep, third part distal to the muscle (branches = 1, 2, 3)
Superior thoracic artery
Thoraco-acromial artery and lateral thoracic artery
Subscapular artery (largest) and the anterior + posterior circumflex humeral arteries
From the lower border of teres major down the medial arm to the cubital fossa, where it divides at the neck of the radius
Radial and ulnar arteries

cards.front: Brachial artery — main branch in the arm?
cards.back: Profunda brachii (deep artery of the arm), which accompanies the radial nerve in the radial groove
May be injured by a supracondylar humeral fracture, risking Volkmann's ischaemic contracture
Runs down the lateral forearm; the pulse is palpated lateral to flexor carpi radialis; it then crosses the snuffbox to form the DEEP palmar arch
Runs down the medial forearm with the ulnar nerve; gives the common interosseous artery and forms the SUPERFICIAL palmar arch

cards.front: Superficial palmar arch — main supply and level?
cards.back: Mainly the ulnar artery; lies across the palm level with the distal border of the extended thumb
Mainly the radial artery (with the deep branch of the ulnar artery); lies proximal to the superficial arch

cards.front: Allen's test — what does it assess?
cards.back: Patency of the radial and ulnar arteries and the palmar arches before radial artery cannulation
Ascends on the lateral (radial) side of the limb, in the deltopectoral groove, then pierces the clavipectoral fascia to join the axillary vein
Ascends on the medial (ulnar) side; pierces the deep fascia in the mid-arm to become (with the venae comitantes) the axillary vein
Connects cephalic to basilic in the cubital fossa; the common site for venepuncture
On the dorsum of the hand; drains laterally to the cephalic and medially to the basilic vein

cards.front: Dermatome — regimental badge area over the deltoid?
cards.back: C5
C6
C7
C8
T1

cards.front: Dermatome — medial arm / floor of axilla?
cards.back: T2 (intercostobrachial nerve)

cards.front: Dermatome landmark trio — thumb, middle, little finger?
cards.back: Thumb = C6, middle finger = C7, little finger = C8 (count 6-7-8 across the hand)
The axillary lymph nodes, then the subclavian lymph trunk
Lie above the medial epicondyle and drain the ulnar (medial) fingers and forearm before the axillary nodes
Anterior (pectoral), posterior (subscapular), lateral (humeral), central and apical groups
Receive ~75% of lymph from the breast; the main route for breast-cancer spread (hence axillary clearance)
Radial nerve (or posterior interosseous) — e.g. mid-shaft humeral fracture or 'Saturday night palsy'
Median nerve — thenar wasting with the thumb adducted in the plane of the palm (loss of opposition)

cards.front: Hand of benediction — nerve and when seen?
cards.back: High median nerve lesion — the lateral fingers cannot flex when making a fist
Ulnar nerve — hyperextended MCPs with flexed IPs of the ring and little fingers
A proximal ulnar lesion causes LESS clawing than a distal one, because medial FDP is also paralysed

cards.front: Froment's sign — positive in which palsy?
cards.back: Ulnar nerve palsy (weak adductor pollicis; the thumb flexes at the IP joint to hold paper)
Long thoracic nerve → serratus anterior (medial border of scapula lifts off the chest)

cards.front: Erb–Duchenne palsy — roots, cause and posture?
cards.back: Upper trunk C5–C6 (excessive shoulder–neck angle at birth or a fall); 'waiter's tip' — arm adducted, medially rotated, forearm pronated

cards.front: Klumpke's palsy — roots, cause and result?
cards.back: Lower trunk C8–T1 (forced arm abduction); a clawed hand ± Horner's syndrome
Fracture of the distal radius with DORSAL displacement — the 'dinner-fork' deformity (usually a fall on the outstretched hand)

cards.front: Smith's fracture — how does it differ from Colles'?
cards.back: Distal radius fracture with VOLAR (palmar) displacement — the 'reverse Colles' ('garden-spade' deformity)
Avascular necrosis of the proximal pole because of its retrograde (distal-to-proximal) blood supply; snuffbox tenderness

cards.front: Surgical neck of humerus fracture — nerve/vessel at risk?
cards.back: Axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery

cards.front: Mid-shaft humeral fracture — nerve at risk?
cards.back: Radial nerve in the radial groove → wrist drop
Brachial artery and median nerve → risk of Volkmann's ischaemic contracture

cards.front: Medial epicondyle fracture — nerve at risk?
cards.back: Ulnar nerve (runs behind the medial epicondyle)
Monteggia = proximal ulnar fracture + radial head dislocation; Galeazzi = distal radial fracture + distal radio-ulnar dislocation

cards.front: Clavicle fracture — commonest site and displacement?
cards.back: Junction of middle and lateral thirds; medial fragment elevated by sternocleidomastoid, lateral fragment dropped by the limb's weight

cards.front: Carpal tunnel syndrome — nerve and features?
cards.back: Median nerve compression under the flexor retinaculum: nocturnal pain, sensory loss of the lateral 3½ fingers (thenar skin spared), thenar wasting

cards.front: Carpal tunnel syndrome — two provocation tests?
cards.back: Tinel's sign (tapping over the nerve) and Phalen's test (sustained wrist flexion)

cards.front: Cubital tunnel syndrome — nerve and site?
cards.back: Ulnar nerve compression behind the medial epicondyle

cards.front: Rotator cuff tear — commonest tendon and sign?
cards.back: Supraspinatus; a painful arc of abduction (~60–120°)
Forearm compartment ischaemia (often after supracondylar fracture/brachial artery injury) → flexor fibrosis and a clawed hand
Progressive fibrosis of the palmar aponeurosis, typically drawing the ring and little fingers into fixed flexion
Avulsion of the extensor tendon at the distal phalanx — the DIP joint droops and cannot extend
Stenosing tenosynovitis at the A1 pulley causing the finger to catch/lock in flexion

cards.front: Thoracic outlet syndrome — what is compressed?
cards.back: The lower trunk of the brachial plexus (C8–T1) and/or the subclavian vessels, often by a cervical rib or scalene muscles — causing medial-hand symptoms and vascular signs.
An extra rib from C7 that can compress the lower trunk/subclavian artery (a cause of thoracic outlet syndrome).

cards.front: De Quervain's tenosynovitis — tendons and test?
cards.back: Stenosing tenosynovitis of abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis at the radial styloid; Finkelstein's test reproduces the pain.
Rupture of the ulnar collateral ligament of the thumb MCP joint, causing pinch weakness and instability.
An intra-articular fracture-dislocation of the base of the 1st metacarpal (thumb); Rolando's is its comminuted form.
A fracture of the neck of the 5th metacarpal, typically from punching with a clenched fist.

cards.front: Radial tunnel syndrome vs tennis elbow?
cards.back: Radial tunnel = compression of the posterior interosseous nerve causing pain distal to the lateral epicondyle without weakness; tennis elbow (lateral epicondylitis) is tendinous and tender directly over the epicondyle.
The common extensor origin (especially extensor carpi radialis brevis) — pain on resisted wrist extension.
The common flexor origin — pain on resisted wrist flexion/pronation.
Ulnar nerve compression between the pisiform and hook of hamate (e.g. cycling), affecting the hand's ulnar-innervated muscles with the dorsal hand sensation spared.

cards.front: Empty-can (Jobe) test — what does it isolate?
cards.back: Supraspinatus — weakness/pain on resisted elevation with the thumb pointing down.

cards.front: Drop-arm test — what does it suggest?
cards.back: A rotator cuff (supraspinatus) tear — the patient cannot lower the abducted arm smoothly.
Global restriction of both active and passive glenohumeral movement from capsular fibrosis/contracture.
Swan-neck = PIP hyperextension with DIP flexion; boutonnière = PIP flexion with DIP hyperextension (central slip rupture).
The flexor digitorum profundus tendon from the distal phalanx (loss of active DIP flexion), classically gripping a jersey.

cards.front: Brachial plexus block — three common approaches?
cards.back: Interscalene, supraclavicular and axillary approaches (each anaesthetises a different level for upper-limb surgery).
In the deltopectoral groove it is used for pacemaker lead insertion and central venous access, and as a superficial cannulation/cutdown site.

cards.cloze: The {{c1::musculocutaneous}} nerve pierces coracobrachialis and supplies the anterior compartment of the arm.
The only muscle that flexes the {{c1::distal interphalangeal}} joints is flexor digitorum profundus.
The carpal tunnel transmits the median nerve and {{c1::nine}} flexor tendons.
The 'LOAF' thenar muscles are supplied by the {{c1::median}} nerve.
The dorsum of the hand over the first web space is supplied by the {{c1::radial}} nerve.
The {{c1::scaphoid}} is the most commonly fractured carpal bone and risks avascular necrosis.
The most commonly dislocated carpal bone is the {{c1::lunate}}.
The superficial palmar arch is completed mainly by the {{c1::ulnar}} artery.
The deep palmar arch is formed mainly by the {{c1::radial}} artery.
The quadrangular space transmits the axillary nerve and the {{c1::posterior circumflex humeral}} artery.
A mid-shaft humeral fracture endangers the {{c1::radial}} nerve, causing wrist drop.
A supracondylar fracture may injure the brachial artery, risking {{c1::Volkmann's ischaemic contracture}}.
The middle finger lies in the {{c1::C7}} dermatome.
{{c1::Supraspinatus}} initiates the first 15° of arm abduction and is the most commonly torn cuff tendon.
The shoulder most commonly dislocates in the {{c1::antero-inferior}} direction, endangering the axillary nerve.

mcqs.stem: The posterior cord of the brachial plexus does NOT give rise to which nerve?

options.why: Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.
Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.
The musculocutaneous nerve arises from the LATERAL cord. The posterior cord gives the upper subscapular, thoracodorsal, lower subscapular, axillary and radial nerves.
Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.

explanation: The musculocutaneous nerve arises from the LATERAL cord. The posterior cord gives the upper subscapular, thoracodorsal, lower subscapular, axillary and radial nerves.
keyFacts: Posterior cord branches: ULTRA — Upper subscapular, (thoraco)dorsal, Lower subscapular, Radial, Axillary
mcqs.teachingPoint: Posterior cord branches: ULTRA — Upper subscapular, (thoraco)dorsal, Lower subscapular, Radial, Axillary

mcqs.stem: A patient cannot abduct the arm from 15° to 90° and has numbness over the lateral shoulder. Which nerve is injured?

options.why: Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.
The axillary nerve supplies deltoid (abduction 15–90°) and gives sensation to the regimental-badge area over the deltoid.
Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.
Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.

explanation: The axillary nerve supplies deltoid (abduction 15–90°) and gives sensation to the regimental-badge area over the deltoid.
keyFacts: Axillary nerve = deltoid + teres minor + lateral shoulder skin
mcqs.teachingPoint: Axillary nerve = deltoid + teres minor + lateral shoulder skin

mcqs.stem: Which muscle is NOT supplied by the median nerve?

options.why: Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.
Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.
Adductor pollicis is supplied by the deep branch of the ULNAR nerve. The median nerve supplies the thenar 'LOAF' muscles and FPL.
Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.

explanation: Adductor pollicis is supplied by the deep branch of the ULNAR nerve. The median nerve supplies the thenar 'LOAF' muscles and FPL.
keyFacts: Ulnar hand muscles: all interossei, hypothenar, adductor pollicis, medial 2 lumbricals
mcqs.teachingPoint: Ulnar hand muscles: all interossei, hypothenar, adductor pollicis, medial 2 lumbricals

mcqs.stem: Which muscle is the ONLY one able to flex the distal interphalangeal joints?

options.why: Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.
Flexor digitorum profundus inserts on the distal phalanges and is the only flexor of the DIP joints.
Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.
Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.

explanation: Flexor digitorum profundus inserts on the distal phalanges and is the only flexor of the DIP joints.
keyFacts: FDS → middle phalanges (PIP); FDP → distal phalanges (DIP)
mcqs.teachingPoint: FDS → middle phalanges (PIP); FDP → distal phalanges (DIP)

mcqs.stem: Which structure does NOT pass through the carpal tunnel?

options.why: Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.
Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.
The ulnar nerve passes SUPERFICIAL to the flexor retinaculum in Guyon's canal, not through the carpal tunnel.
Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.

explanation: The ulnar nerve passes SUPERFICIAL to the flexor retinaculum in Guyon's canal, not through the carpal tunnel.
keyFacts: Carpal tunnel = median nerve + 9 tendons (4 FDS, 4 FDP, 1 FPL)
mcqs.teachingPoint: Carpal tunnel = median nerve + 9 tendons (4 FDS, 4 FDP, 1 FPL)

mcqs.stem: The most commonly fractured carpal bone, prone to avascular necrosis, is the:

options.why: Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.
The scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone; its retrograde blood supply risks avascular necrosis of the proximal pole. Snuffbox tenderness is the clue.
Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.
Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.

explanation: The scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone; its retrograde blood supply risks avascular necrosis of the proximal pole. Snuffbox tenderness is the clue.
keyFacts: Scaphoid fracture → snuffbox tenderness → AVN of proximal pole
mcqs.teachingPoint: Scaphoid fracture → snuffbox tenderness → AVN of proximal pole

mcqs.stem: The contents of the quadrangular space are the:

options.why: Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.

options.text: Axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery
options.why: The quadrangular space transmits the axillary nerve and the posterior circumflex humeral artery around the surgical neck of the humerus.
Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.
Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.

explanation: The quadrangular space transmits the axillary nerve and the posterior circumflex humeral artery around the surgical neck of the humerus.
keyFacts: Quadrangular space = axillary nerve + posterior circumflex humeral artery
mcqs.teachingPoint: Quadrangular space = axillary nerve + posterior circumflex humeral artery

mcqs.stem: Biceps brachii is MOST powerful as a:

options.why: Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.
With the elbow flexed, biceps brachii is the most powerful supinator of the forearm (as well as an elbow flexor).
Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.
Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.

explanation: With the elbow flexed, biceps brachii is the most powerful supinator of the forearm (as well as an elbow flexor).
keyFacts: Biceps = supination + elbow flexion; nerve = musculocutaneous
mcqs.teachingPoint: Biceps = supination + elbow flexion; nerve = musculocutaneous

mcqs.stem: The second part of the axillary artery lies:

options.why: Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.
Pectoralis minor crosses the axillary artery and divides it into three parts; the second part lies deep to the muscle and gives the thoraco-acromial and lateral thoracic arteries.
Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.
Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.

explanation: Pectoralis minor crosses the axillary artery and divides it into three parts; the second part lies deep to the muscle and gives the thoraco-acromial and lateral thoracic arteries.
keyFacts: Parts 1-2-3 give 1-2-3 branches; number of branches = part number
mcqs.teachingPoint: Parts 1-2-3 give 1-2-3 branches; number of branches = part number

mcqs.stem: A deep laceration behind the medial epicondyle would most likely produce:

options.why: Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.

options.text: Claw hand affecting the ring and little fingers
options.why: The ulnar nerve lies behind the medial epicondyle; injury causes clawing of the ring and little fingers (with sensory loss over the medial 1½ digits).
Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.
Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.

explanation: The ulnar nerve lies behind the medial epicondyle; injury causes clawing of the ring and little fingers (with sensory loss over the medial 1½ digits).
keyFacts: Ulnar nerve behind medial epicondyle → claw hand
mcqs.teachingPoint: Ulnar nerve behind medial epicondyle → claw hand

mcqs.stem: Which rotator-cuff muscle initiates abduction of the arm?

options.why: Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.
Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.
Supraspinatus initiates the first 15° of abduction before the deltoid takes over; it is the most commonly torn cuff muscle.
Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.

explanation: Supraspinatus initiates the first 15° of abduction before the deltoid takes over; it is the most commonly torn cuff muscle.
keyFacts: SITS: Supraspinatus (abduct/initiate), Infraspinatus & Teres minor (lateral rotation), Subscapularis (medial rotation)
mcqs.teachingPoint: SITS: Supraspinatus (abduct/initiate), Infraspinatus & Teres minor (lateral rotation), Subscapularis (medial rotation)

mcqs.stem: A 'waiter's tip' posture (adducted, medially rotated arm, pronated forearm) indicates injury to:

options.why: Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.
Erb–Duchenne palsy is an upper-trunk (C5–C6) injury producing the 'waiter's tip' posture from loss of deltoid, biceps and the lateral rotators.
Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.
Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.

explanation: Erb–Duchenne palsy is an upper-trunk (C5–C6) injury producing the 'waiter's tip' posture from loss of deltoid, biceps and the lateral rotators.
keyFacts: Upper trunk = Erb's = waiter's tip; Lower trunk = Klumpke's = claw hand
mcqs.teachingPoint: Upper trunk = Erb's = waiter's tip; Lower trunk = Klumpke's = claw hand

mcqs.stem: The usual direction of glenohumeral dislocation and the nerve most at risk are:

options.why: Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.
The shoulder usually dislocates antero-inferiorly (the capsule is weakest and unsupported by cuff inferiorly), endangering the axillary nerve.
Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.
Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.

explanation: The shoulder usually dislocates antero-inferiorly (the capsule is weakest and unsupported by cuff inferiorly), endangering the axillary nerve.

mcqs.stem: Unassisted supination of the extended forearm is produced mainly by the:

options.why: Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.
With the elbow EXTENDED, biceps is ineffective, so the supinator produces supination. Biceps supinates powerfully only with the elbow flexed.
Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.
Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.

explanation: With the elbow EXTENDED, biceps is ineffective, so the supinator produces supination. Biceps supinates powerfully only with the elbow flexed.
keyFacts: Supinator = supination with elbow extended; supplied by deep radial (PIN)
mcqs.teachingPoint: Supinator = supination with elbow extended; supplied by deep radial (PIN)

mcqs.stem: The anatomical snuffbox floor is formed mainly by the:

options.why: Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.
The floor of the snuffbox is the scaphoid and trapezium; the radial artery crosses it, and deep tenderness suggests a scaphoid fracture.
Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.
Not the best answer here — see the explanation below.

explanation: The floor of the snuffbox is the scaphoid and trapezium; the radial artery crosses it, and deep tenderness suggests a scaphoid fracture.
keyFacts: Snuffbox: APL/EPB (lateral), EPL (medial), floor scaphoid+trapezium, radial artery within
mcqs.teachingPoint: Snuffbox: APL/EPB (lateral), EPL (medial), floor scaphoid+trapezium, radial artery within

mcqs.teachingPoint: De Quervain's = APL + EPB (1st dorsal compartment)
